title: Reversible reactions and dynamic equilibrium
html:
Guiding question

How can the extent of a reversible reaction be influenced? Many reactions do not go to completion: they reach a state of dynamic equilibrium in which reactants and products coexist. The equilibrium constant, K, tells you how far a reaction goes; Le Châtelier's principle predicts how the mixture responds when conditions change. At HL you calculate K and equilibrium concentrations, use the reaction quotient Q, and link K to Gibbs energy.

CodeUnderstanding
R2.3.1A state of dynamic equilibrium is reached in a closed system when the rates of the forward and backward reactions are equal.
R2.3.2The equilibrium law describes how the equilibrium constant, K, can be determined from the stoichiometry of a reaction.
R2.3.3The magnitude of K indicates the extent of a reaction at equilibrium and is temperature dependent.
R2.3.4Le Châtelier's principle: changes in conditions shift the position of equilibrium; a catalyst does not.
R2.3.5 AHLThe reaction quotient, Q, and the direction a reaction takes to reach equilibrium.
R2.3.6 AHLSolving equilibrium problems: K and equilibrium concentrations from given data.
R2.3.7 AHLThe equilibrium constant and Gibbs energy are related: ΔG° = −RT ln K.

R2.3.1 Dynamic equilibrium

Start with the class "do now": N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃. The double arrow ⇌ means the reaction is reversible: ammonia forms from nitrogen and hydrogen, and at the same time ammonia breaks back down. The enthalpy change applies to both directions with opposite signs: forming ammonia releases 45.9 kJ per mole of NH₃ (−91.8 kJ for 2NH₃ as written), so decomposing it absorbs the same amount.

A reversible reaction can go in both directions, shown by ⇌. When it starts, the forward rate is high (lots of reactant) and the reverse rate is zero (no product). As reactants are used up the forward rate falls; as products build up the reverse rate rises. Eventually the two rates become equal.

Key point · characteristics of dynamic equilibrium (learn these four)
  1. The rate of the forward reaction equals the rate of the reverse reaction.
  2. The concentrations of reactants and products remain constant (not equal).
  3. It is reached only in a closed system (no matter exchanged with the surroundings).
  4. There is no change in macroscopic properties such as colour, density or pressure.

"Dynamic" means both reactions are still happening at the particle level; nothing has stopped. The class analogy: running on the spot on a down escalator. You stay in the same place only because your effort exactly matches the escalator.

  • The same equilibrium mixture can be reached starting from the reactants or from the products (e.g. starting with pure HI, or with H₂ + I₂).
  • Physical changes can also be equilibria: in a sealed bottle of water or ethanol, the rate of evaporation equals the rate of condensation; a mixture of ice and water at 0 °C has equal rates of melting and freezing.
  • The fizzy drink "mystery" from class: in a sealed bottle CO₂(g) + H₂O(l) ⇌ H₂CO₃(aq) is at equilibrium. Opening the bottle makes it an open system, CO₂ escapes and the equilibrium keeps shifting left, so the drink goes flat.
Common mistakeWriting "the concentrations of reactants and products are equal" or "the reaction has stopped" loses the mark. At equilibrium the yield need not be 50% and the amounts of ice and water need not be equal.

Graphs. A concentration–time graph shows reactant curves falling and product curves rising until both become horizontal at the same time (equilibrium reached). A rate–time graph shows the forward rate falling from a high value and the reverse rate rising from zero until they merge into one horizontal line.

In this example HI decomposes, 2HI(g) ⇌ H₂(g) + I₂(g), while H₂ and I₂ recombine. Equilibrium is reached when HI decomposes as fast as it re-forms. Notice the stoichiometry: each mole of H₂ formed uses 2 mol of HI, so [HI] falls by 2 × 0.107 = 0.214 mol dm⁻³, from 1.000 to 0.786 mol dm⁻³.

Use the graph to calculate K for 2HI ⇌ H₂ + I₂ (K = [H₂][I₂] ÷ [HI]²).

K = (0.107 × 0.107) ÷ 0.786² = 0.01145 ÷ 0.6178 = 0.0185. K < 1, so the equilibrium lies to the left (mostly HI). For the reverse reaction, H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI, K = 1 ÷ 0.0185 = 54.

Which statement about a system at dynamic equilibrium is correct?

  1. The forward and reverse reactions have both stopped
  2. The concentrations of reactants and products are equal
  3. The rates of the forward and reverse reactions are equal
  4. It can be reached in an open beaker

Both reactions continue at equal rates, so concentrations stay constant (but are not usually equal). Matter must not escape, so it needs a closed system.

Equilibrium can only be established in a closed system, and at equilibrium the concentrations are constant.

title: Le Châtelier's principle and industrial equilibria
html:
R2.3.4 Le Châtelier's principle

DefinitionLe Châtelier's principle: if a system at equilibrium is disturbed by a change in conditions, the position of equilibrium shifts to oppose (minimize) the change.

Class mnemonic: equilibrium "doesn't like change". Make it hotter → it moves to cool down (endothermic direction). Make it colder → it moves to warm up (exothermic direction). Raise the pressure → it moves to lower it (fewer gas molecules). Lower the pressure → it moves to raise it (more gas molecules). Add a chemical → it moves to use it up. Remove a chemical → it moves to make more.

"Shifts to the right" = forward reaction favoured, more products. "Shifts to the left" = reverse reaction favoured, more reactants.

The class cone game models this: two teams flip cones "up" and "down" at the same time. Adding players to one team changes the ratio of up to down cones (like changing a concentration); a "cheerleader" who speeds up both teams equally changes how fast cones flip but not the final ratio (a catalyst).

ChangeEffect on position of equilibriumEffect on K
Increase [reactant] or remove productShifts rightNo change
Increase [product] or remove reactantShifts leftNo change
Increase pressure (decrease volume)Shifts to the side with fewer gas moleculesNo change
Decrease pressure (increase volume)Shifts to the side with more gas moleculesNo change
Increase temperatureShifts in the endothermic directionChanges (increases if forward is endothermic)
Decrease temperatureShifts in the exothermic directionChanges (increases if forward is exothermic)
Add a catalystNo change; equilibrium is reached fasterNo change

Why concentration changes don't change K: adding reactant makes the ratio [products]/[reactants] (Q) smaller than K, so the forward reaction runs until the ratio equals K again. Why temperature does change K: the forward and reverse reactions have different activation energies, so a temperature change speeds them up by different amounts and a new ratio is set up.

Mini review: A(g) + B(g) ⇌ C(g), forward reaction exothermic. Which way does the equilibrium shift if you (a) increase the pressure, (b) decrease the pressure, (c) increase the temperature, (d) decrease the temperature, (e) increase [A], (f) decrease [A]? Decide, then reveal.(a) Right: 2 gas molecules → 1. (b) Left: towards more gas molecules. (c) Left: the endothermic (reverse) direction absorbs the added heat. (d) Right: the exothermic direction releases heat. (e) Right: to use up the added A. (f) Left: to make more A.

Concentration: the cobalt chloride equilibrium

[Co(H₂O)₆]²⁺(aq) (pink) + 4Cl⁻(aq) ⇌ [CoCl₄]²⁻(aq) (blue) + 6H₂O(l)
ChangeShiftColour
Add Cl⁻ (e.g. conc. HCl)Right, to use up Cl⁻Blue
Add H₂OLeft, to use up waterPink
Remove Cl⁻ (e.g. add Ag⁺ to precipitate AgCl)Left, to replace Cl⁻Pink

Concentrated HCl is added to pink [Co(H₂O)₆]²⁺ solution. What colour change is seen and why?

  1. Pink to blue: added Cl⁻ shifts the equilibrium right
  2. Blue to pink: H⁺ ions shift the equilibrium left
  3. No change: K is unchanged
  4. Pink to colourless: the complex is destroyed

Adding Cl⁻ (a reactant) shifts the position right to use it up, forming blue [CoCl₄]²⁻. K is unchanged, but the position moves.

Temperature

For N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g) the forward reaction is exothermic (ΔH = −92 kJ as written, i.e. −46 kJ per mole of NH₃) and the reverse reaction endothermic (+92 kJ). Raising the temperature shifts the equilibrium in the endothermic direction (left, less ammonia) to absorb heat; lowering it shifts it in the exothermic direction (right) to release heat.

Worked example · 2 · colour equilibria from class[Co(H₂O)₆]²⁺ (pink) + 4Cl⁻ ⇌ [CoCl₄]²⁻ (blue) + 6H₂O, forward endothermic
Add conc. HCl (Cl⁻) → shifts right → blue. Add water → shifts left → pink. Heat → endothermic direction (right) → blue; cool → pink.
2NO₂ (brown) ⇌ N₂O₄ (colourless), forward exothermic
Heat → shifts left → darker brown. Increase pressure → shifts right (2 → 1 gas molecules) → paler (after an initial darkening as the gas is compressed).

Pressure

Pressure: count gas molecules only. If both sides have the same number (e.g. H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI, CO + H₂O ⇌ H₂ + CO₂), pressure has no effect on the position. Adding water to an aqueous equilibrium with equal numbers of dissolved particles on each side has no effect either.

For which equilibrium does increasing the pressure have no effect on the position of equilibrium?

  1. 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g)
  2. N₂O₄(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g)
  3. H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g)
  4. N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g)

H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI has 2 gas molecules on each side, so neither direction lowers the pressure. The others all change the number of gas molecules.

Key point · catalystsA catalyst lowers the activation energy of the forward and reverse reactions equally, so both rates increase by the same factor. The position of equilibrium and K are unchanged; equilibrium is simply reached sooner. A claim that a new catalyst "increases the yield of ammonia" is therefore invalid.
Worked example · 3 · reagents that react with a species2Br⁻(aq) + H₂O₂(aq) + 2H⁺(aq) ⇌ Br₂(aq) + 2H₂O(l). Adding NaOH removes H⁺ (neutralization), so the equilibrium shifts left and the red-brown colour fades. Adding HCl adds H⁺, so it shifts right and the colour deepens.

Le Châtelier's principle: when conditions change, the position of equilibrium shifts to oppose the change.

Industrial equilibria: compromise conditions

Le Châtelier tells you the conditions for the highest equilibrium yield; industry must also consider rate, cost and safety.

Haber processContact process (key step)
EquationN₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), ΔH = −92 kJ2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g), ΔH = −196 kJ
Best yieldLow T, high p (4 → 2 gas molecules)Low T, high p (3 → 2 gas molecules)
Conditions used~450–500 °C, ~200 atm, iron catalyst~450 °C, 1–2 atm, V₂O₅ catalyst
WhyLow T gives a high yield but too slow a rate, so a moderate T is a compromise. Very high pressure is expensive (thick pipes, compressors) and dangerous. NH₃ is removed by liquefaction and unreacted gases recycled.Conversion is already over 95% at low pressure, so expensive high pressure is unnecessary. 450 °C gives a fast enough rate.
Exam-style: (a) How do the raw materials air and natural gas affect the sustainability of the process? (b) Use ideas about energy to explain how the iron catalyst works. (c) The reaction is reversible, yet almost all the N₂ and H₂ end up as ammonia. Explain using the flow chart. Answer, then reveal the mark points.(a) Air makes the process more sustainable because its supply is effectively unlimited/renewable; natural gas makes it less sustainable because it is a finite fossil resource. (b) The catalyst provides an alternative route (pathway) with a lower activation energy, so less energy is needed to start breaking bonds. (Explanations based only on collisions were not credited.) (c) Unreacted N₂ and H₂ are recycled through the reactor; ammonia is removed, so the system never settles at equilibrium and keeps shifting to the right.
Exam tipDo not score with the single word "compromise". Explain both halves: "a lower temperature would give a higher yield but the rate would be too slow; a higher pressure would increase the yield but the cost of equipment and energy would be too high." Do not just say "because of Le Châtelier's principle"; state the direction and the reason (number of gas molecules, or exothermic/endothermic).

Why is the Haber process run at about 450 °C rather than at room temperature, even though a lower temperature gives a higher equilibrium yield?

  1. At low temperature the equilibrium lies to the left
  2. At low temperature the rate is too slow to be economic
  3. The iron catalyst only lowers ΔH at high temperature
  4. High temperature increases K for this reaction

The forward reaction is exothermic, so low T favours ammonia, but the rate would be far too slow. 450 °C is a compromise between yield and rate. K actually decreases as T rises for this reaction.

TOKFritz Haber's process feeds roughly half the world through fertilizers, yet he also developed chlorine gas as a weapon in the First World War, and ammonia from his process was oxidized to nitric acid for explosives. His involvement in chemical warfare had tragic personal consequences too. Should scientists be held responsible for how their discoveries are used?

title: The equilibrium constant K
html:
R2.3.2 The equilibrium law

Class "do now": how could you find out by experiment whether an equilibrium favours the forward or the reverse reaction? You would measure the equilibrium concentrations (by colour, titration or pressure) and put them into the equilibrium expression. The size of the answer, K, tells you.

aA + bB ⇌ cC + dDK = [C]c[D]d[A]a[B]b
  • Products on top, reactants on the bottom.
  • Square brackets mean equilibrium concentration in mol dm⁻³. Round brackets lose the mark.
  • Each concentration is raised to the power of its coefficient in the balanced equation.
  • K is specific to the equation as written and to the temperature.
  • IB questions focus on homogeneous equilibria (all species in the same phase). Pure solids (and pure liquids not acting as a solvent) are left out of the expression. In a heterogeneous system the species are in different phases.
Worked example · 1 · writing expressionsN₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g): K = [NH₃]² ÷ ([N₂][H₂]³)
2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g): K = [SO₃]² ÷ ([SO₂]²[O₂])
CH₃COOH(l) + C₂H₅OH(l) ⇌ CH₃COOC₂H₅(l) + H₂O(l): K = [CH₃COOC₂H₅][H₂O] ÷ ([CH₃COOH][C₂H₅OH])

What is the equilibrium expression for 2NO(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g)?

  1. K = [NO₂] ÷ ([NO][O₂])
  2. K = [NO₂]² ÷ ([NO]²[O₂])
  3. K = ([NO]²[O₂]) ÷ [NO₂]²
  4. K = 2[NO₂] ÷ (2[NO][O₂])

Products over reactants, each raised to the power of its coefficient. Coefficients become powers, never multipliers.

Class questions: write K expressions for (1) the formation of ammonia, (2) CH₃COOH + CH₃OH ⇌ CH₃COOCH₃ + H₂O, (3) the complete combustion of methane at a temperature where water is a gas, (4) C(s) + O₂(g) ⇌ CO₂(g), (5) CaCO₃(s) ⇌ CaO(s) + CO₂(g). Then reveal.(1) K = [NH₃]² ÷ ([N₂][H₂]³). (2) K = [CH₃COOCH₃][H₂O] ÷ ([CH₃COOH][CH₃OH]). (3) CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) ⇌ CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(g): K = [CO₂][H₂O]² ÷ ([CH₄][O₂]²). (4) and (5) are heterogeneous: leaving out the solids gives K = [CO₂] ÷ [O₂] and K = [CO₂]. (Heterogeneous examples are for interest; IB questions use homogeneous systems.)

Units of K. The 2025 guide treats K as dimensionless, but older questions sometimes ask for units: substitute mol dm⁻³ for each term and cancel. For Fe³⁺(aq) + SCN⁻(aq) ⇌ FeSCN²⁺(aq), K has units (mol dm⁻³) ÷ (mol dm⁻³)² = mol⁻¹ dm³. When there are equal numbers of concentration terms top and bottom (e.g. the ester equilibrium) the units cancel.

If units were required, what would they be for K of N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g)?

  1. No units
  2. mol⁻² dm⁶
  3. mol² dm⁻⁶
  4. mol⁻¹ dm³

(mol dm⁻³)² ÷ (mol dm⁻³)⁴ = (mol dm⁻³)⁻² = mol⁻² dm⁶. Two concentration terms on top, four underneath.

Manipulating K (from the HL lessons):

Change to the equationNew KExample
Reverse it1/KH₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI, K = 794; 2HI ⇌ H₂ + I₂, K = 1/794 = 1.26 × 10⁻³
Multiply all coefficients by 2K²2H₂ + 2I₂ ⇌ 4HI, K = 794²
Halve all coefficients√K½H₂ + ½I₂ ⇌ HI, K = √794 = 28.2
Add two equationsK₁ × K₂Overall K for a sequence of steps = product of the step K values

For the Haber process, N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃, K = 9.60 at 573 K. What is K for 2NH₃ ⇌ N₂ + 3H₂ at 573 K?

Reversing the equation inverts K: 1 ÷ 9.60 = 0.104.

R2.3.3 The magnitude of K

Value of KPosition of equilibrium
K ≫ 1 (e.g. > 10³)Lies far to the right; reaction goes almost to completion; mostly products.
K > 1Products favoured.
K ≈ 1Significant amounts of both reactants and products.
K < 1Reactants favoured.
K ≪ 1 (e.g. < 10⁻³)Lies far to the left; reaction hardly proceeds; mostly reactants.
  • K depends only on temperature. Concentration, pressure and catalysts do not change it.
  • K says nothing about rate. A reaction with a huge K can be extremely slow (high Ea).
  • Stronger acids have larger K values for dissociation (Reactivity 3.1).
Exam tipTo decide whether a reaction is exo- or endothermic from K values: if K increases with temperature, raising T favoured the forward reaction, so the forward reaction is endothermic. Example: CO₂ + H₂ ⇌ H₂O + CO has K = 1.1 at 850 °C and 4.9 at 1700 °C, so it is endothermic.

For 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g), ΔH = −196 kJ. What happens to K when the temperature is raised?

  1. K increases
  2. K decreases
  3. K is unchanged because K is a constant
  4. K increases only if pressure is also raised

Raising T shifts the equilibrium in the endothermic (reverse) direction, so there is less SO₃ at equilibrium and K falls. Temperature is the only factor that changes K.

The only factor that changes the value of K is temperature.

Typical exam questions and how to answer them

  • State two characteristics of dynamic equilibrium: rates of forward and reverse reactions equal; concentrations constant (closed system; no change in macroscopic properties).
  • Predict and explain a shift (2 marks): one mark for the direction, one for the reason (e.g. "shifts right; fewer moles of gas on the right").
  • State and explain the effect of a catalyst on K and rate (4 marks): no effect on K/position; forward and reverse rates increase equally; increases rate; alternative pathway with lower Ea.
  • Explain the effect of temperature on K (2 marks): direction of change of K; link to the sign of ΔH.
  • Sketch rate–time for forward and reverse reactions: forward starts high and falls; reverse starts at zero and rises; they meet and become one horizontal line.

title: Q and equilibrium calculations (HL)
html:
R2.3.5 The reaction quotient, Q AHL

Q has exactly the same expression as K but uses concentrations at any moment, not necessarily at equilibrium. Comparing Q with K tells you which way the reaction must go to reach equilibrium.

ComparisonMeaningNet reaction
Q < KToo few productsForward (shifts right)
Q = KAt equilibriumNo net change
Q > KToo many productsReverse (shifts left)
Worked example · 4 · direction of change (class worksheet style)2NO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2NO₃(g), K = 42.5 at 923 °C. Mixed in 1.00 dm³: 0.0500 mol NO₂, 0.122 mol O₂, 0.300 mol NO₃.
Q = 0.300² ÷ (0.0500² × 0.122) = 0.0900 ÷ 3.05 × 10⁻⁴ = 295
Q (295) > K (42.5) → reaction proceeds in the reverse direction (to the left) until Q = K
Q tells you the direction, not how fast equilibrium is reached.

1.00 mol SO₂, 2.00 mol O₂ and 1.00 mol SO₃ are placed in a 1.00 dm³ container. For 2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃, K = 0.282 at this temperature. In which direction does the reaction initially go?

  1. Forward, because Q < K
  2. Reverse, because Q > K
  3. Neither, because Q = K
  4. Forward, because there are more moles of reactants

Q = [SO₃]² ÷ ([SO₂]²[O₂]) = 1.00² ÷ (1.00² × 2.00) = 0.500. Q (0.500) > K (0.282), so the reverse reaction is favoured until Q falls to K. (Mark scheme: Q uses non-equilibrium concentrations, K uses equilibrium concentrations.)

R2.3.6 Equilibrium calculations AHL

Use an ICE table (Initial, Change, Equilibrium). The class motto: "It's all moles!" Work in moles, then divide by the volume to get concentrations before substituting into K.

  1. Write the balanced equation and the K expression.
  2. Fill in initial amounts.
  3. Use the one known equilibrium amount (or x) to find the change; changes must be in the mole ratio (−ax, −bx, +cx, +dx).
  4. Equilibrium = initial + change.
  5. Convert to concentrations (÷ V). If the total number of moles of gas or solute is the same on both sides, V cancels and can be omitted.
  6. Substitute and calculate.
Worked example · 5 · K from one equilibrium amount (class example)0.56 mol NO₂ decomposes in a 0.50 dm³ vessel; 0.48 mol NO is present at equilibrium. 2NO₂ ⇌ 2NO + O₂
2NO₂2NOO₂
Initial / mol0.5600
Change / mol−2x = −0.48+2x = +0.48+x = +0.24
Equilibrium / mol0.080.480.24
Concentration / mol dm⁻³0.160.960.48
K = [NO]²[O₂] ÷ [NO₂]² = 0.96² × 0.48 ÷ 0.16² = 17.3
The key step: 0 + 2x = 0.48, so x = 0.24. Because the question gives the volume (0.50 dm³) and the moles of gas change, you must divide each amount by the volume.

Try it yourself: 2.0 mol A and 1.5 mol B react in 0.80 dm³: 2A + B ⇌ C + 3D. At equilibrium there is 0.50 mol C. Calculate K.

Change: C +x = 0.50, so A −2x = −1.0, B −x = −0.50, D +3x = +1.5.
Equilibrium moles: A 1.0, B 1.0, C 0.50, D 1.5.
Concentrations (÷ 0.80): A 1.25, B 1.25, C 0.625, D 1.875 mol dm⁻³.
K = [C][D]³ ÷ ([A]²[B]) = (0.625 × 1.875³) ÷ (1.25² × 1.25) = 4.12 ÷ 1.95 = 2.11.

H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g). At equilibrium [H₂] = [I₂] = 0.0037 mol dm⁻³ and [HI] = 0.028 mol dm⁻³. Calculate K.

K = [HI]² ÷ ([H₂][I₂]) = 0.028² ÷ (0.0037 × 0.0037) = 7.84 × 10⁻⁴ ÷ 1.37 × 10⁻⁵ = 57.

2.00 mol ethanoic acid and 2.00 mol ethanol reach equilibrium: CH₃CH₂OH + CH₃COOH ⇌ CH₃COOCH₂CH₃ + H₂O. 0.67 mol ethanoic acid remains. Calculate K.

ICE: acid and alcohol 2.00 − x = 0.67, so x = 1.33; ester and water 1.33 each.
K = (1.33 × 1.33) ÷ (0.67 × 0.67) = 3.94. There are equal numbers of moles on each side, so the volume cancels and is not needed.
Worked example · 6 · solving for x (exact)1.00 mol H₂ and 1.00 mol I₂ are heated in 1.00 dm³; K = 64 for H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI. Find [HI].
Equilibrium: [H₂] = [I₂] = 1.00 − x; [HI] = 2x
64 = (2x)² ÷ (1.00 − x)² → take square roots: 8 = 2x ÷ (1.00 − x)
8 − 8x = 2x → x = 0.80 → [HI] = 1.60 mol dm⁻³, [H₂] = [I₂] = 0.20 mol dm⁻³
Taking the square root works when the expression is a perfect square; otherwise look for an approximation.
IB question: 1.50 × 10⁻² mol H₂ and 1.50 × 10⁻² mol I₂ are put in a 2.00 dm³ flask; K = 53.0 for H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI. Find the equilibrium concentrations. Try it, then reveal.[H₂]₀ = [I₂]₀ = 1.50 × 10⁻² ÷ 2.00 = 7.50 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³. At equilibrium [H₂] = [I₂] = 7.50 × 10⁻³ − x, [HI] = 2x.
√53.0 = 7.28 = 2x ÷ (7.50 × 10⁻³ − x) → x = 5.88 × 10⁻³.
[H₂] = [I₂] = 1.62 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³; [HI] = 1.18 × 10⁻² mol dm⁻³.
The examiners noted most marks were lost by forgetting to divide by the 2.00 dm³ volume or by mixing up which expression contains x. No quadratic is needed: take the square root.
Worked example · 7 · very small K approximationCOCl₂(g) ⇌ CO(g) + Cl₂(g), K = 2.2 × 10⁻¹⁰ at 100 °C; [COCl₂]₀ = 0.500 mol dm⁻³.
At equilibrium: [COCl₂] = 0.500 − x ≈ 0.500 (K is very small, so x ≪ 0.500); [CO] = [Cl₂] = x
2.2 × 10⁻¹⁰ = x² ÷ 0.500 → x = √(1.1 × 10⁻¹⁰) = 1.0 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³
State the assumption and why it is valid (K < 10⁻³, so very little reactant is used up). The 2025 guide does not require solving quadratic equations.
Worked example · 8 · IB question (SO₂Cl₂)8.60 × 10⁻³ mol SO₂ and 8.60 × 10⁻³ mol Cl₂ in 1.00 dm³ at 375 °C form 7.65 × 10⁻⁴ mol SO₂Cl₂ at equilibrium. SO₂ + Cl₂ ⇌ SO₂Cl₂, ΔH = −84.5 kJ.
[SO₂] = [Cl₂] = 8.60 × 10⁻³ − 7.65 × 10⁻⁴ = 7.84 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³
K = 7.65 × 10⁻⁴ ÷ (7.84 × 10⁻³)² = 12.5
Cooling to 300 °C: favours the exothermic forward reaction, so [SO₂Cl₂] and K increase. Increasing the volume to 1.50 dm³: shifts left (more gas molecules), so [SO₂Cl₂] decreases, K unchanged. Catalyst: no effect on the equilibrium concentration.

Practice set (class "Kc calculations")

1. 2.00 mol PCl₅ is heated in a 20.0 dm³ vessel; at equilibrium there is 1.20 mol Cl₂. PCl₅ ⇌ PCl₃ + Cl₂. Calculate K.

Equilibrium moles: PCl₅ 2.00 − 1.20 = 0.80; PCl₃ 1.20; Cl₂ 1.20. Concentrations (÷ 20.0): 0.040, 0.060, 0.060.
K = (0.060 × 0.060) ÷ 0.040 = 0.090 (units mol dm⁻³ if asked).

2. 1.00 mol HI is 22% dissociated at 444 °C: 2HI ⇌ H₂ + I₂. Calculate K.

0.22 mol HI dissociates, giving 0.11 mol H₂ and 0.11 mol I₂; 0.78 mol HI remains. The volume cancels (2 mol gas each side).
K = (0.11 × 0.11) ÷ 0.78² = 0.0199.

3. For 2A + B₂ ⇌ 2AB, [A] = 0.0200, [B₂] = 0.100 and [AB] = 0.400 mol dm⁻³ at equilibrium. Calculate K.

K = [AB]² ÷ ([A]²[B₂]) = 0.400² ÷ (0.0200² × 0.100) = 0.160 ÷ 4.00 × 10⁻⁵ = 4000 (mol⁻¹ dm³ if units are asked).

4. For H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI, K = 54.1. At equilibrium [H₂] = 0.480 × 10⁻³ and [HI] = 3.53 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³. Calculate [I₂].

[I₂] = [HI]² ÷ (K × [H₂]) = (3.53 × 10⁻³)² ÷ (54.1 × 0.480 × 10⁻³) = 1.246 × 10⁻⁵ ÷ 0.0260 = 4.80 × 10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³.
Follow-ups: doubling [H₂] shifts the position right with K unchanged; for this endothermic (ΔH > 0) reaction, raising T shifts right and K increases.

5. 1.00 mol steam and 1.00 mol CO reach equilibrium; 33.3% of the mixture is H₂. H₂O + CO ⇌ H₂ + CO₂. Calculate K.

Total moles stay 2.00, so H₂ = 0.667 mol = x; CO₂ = 0.667; H₂O = CO = 0.333 mol. Volume cancels.
K = (0.667 × 0.667) ÷ (0.333 × 0.333) = 4.00.

6. N₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2NO has K = 0.0036 at 2680 K. 1.00 mol N₂ and 1.00 mol O₂ react. What mass of NO (M = 30.01 g mol⁻¹) is present at equilibrium?

Equilibrium: N₂ = O₂ = 1.00 − x, NO = 2x (volume cancels).
0.0036 = (2x)² ÷ (1.00 − x)². This is a perfect square, so take roots: 0.060 = 2x ÷ (1.00 − x) → x = 0.060 ÷ 2.060 = 0.0291.
n(NO) = 2x = 0.0583 mol → mass = 0.0583 × 30.01 = 1.75 g. (The class answer used the quadratic formula and got the same result; the square-root route is quicker and is all the 2025 guide expects.)

title: K and Gibbs energy (HL)
html:
R2.3.7 K and Gibbs energy AHL

ΔG° = −RT ln KK = e−ΔG°/RT

(Data booklet section 1.) R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, T in kelvin. ΔG° is usually given in kJ mol⁻¹, so multiply by 1000 before substituting.

A reacting mixture moves towards equilibrium because its Gibbs energy falls as it goes. Starting from pure reactants, the mixture slides "downhill" in G; at equilibrium G is at its minimum and the driving force for further net change is zero.

ΔG°ln KKEquilibrium mixture
NegativePositive> 1Products favoured (forward reaction spontaneous under standard conditions)
Zero0= 1Neither side favoured
PositiveNegative< 1Reactants favoured

Because the relationship is logarithmic, a small change in ΔG° makes a big change in K: about −5.7 kJ mol⁻¹ at 298 K multiplies K by 10. ΔG° values of a few tens of kJ either way give K values so extreme that the reaction is effectively complete or effectively does not happen. ΔG° can be found from ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS° (Reactivity 1.4) or from ΔG°f values in the data booklet.

A reaction has ΔG° = +10 kJ mol⁻¹ at 298 K. What can you conclude about K?

  1. K > 1, products favoured
  2. K = 1
  3. K < 1, reactants favoured
  4. K is negative

ln K = −ΔG°/RT = −10 000 ÷ (8.31 × 298) = −4.04, so K = 0.018. A positive ΔG° gives a negative ln K and K between 0 and 1. K can never be negative.

Worked example · 9 · K from ΔG°Esterification of ethanoic acid with ethanol: ΔG° = −4.38 kJ mol⁻¹ at 298 K.
ln K = −ΔG° ÷ RT = −(−4380) ÷ (8.31 × 298) = 1.769
K = e1.769 = 5.86 → K > 1, products (ester and water) favoured
Worked example · 10 · ΔG° from KH₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g), K = 794 at 298 K.
ΔG° = −8.31 × 298 × ln 794 = −8.31 × 298 × 6.677 = −1.65 × 10⁴ J mol⁻¹ = −16.5 kJ mol⁻¹
Worked example · 11 · K from ΔG°f values (class example)BaSO₄(s) ⇌ Ba²⁺(aq) + SO₄²⁻(aq). ΔG°f values: Ba²⁺(aq) −560.8, SO₄²⁻(aq) −744.5, BaSO₄(s) −1362.3 kJ mol⁻¹.
ΔG° = (−560.8) + (−744.5) − (−1362.3) = +57.0 kJ mol⁻¹
ln K = −57 000 ÷ (8.31 × 298) = −23.0 → K = e−23.0 = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁰
This matches the measured value (1.1 × 10⁻¹⁰) for this sparingly soluble salt: the positive ΔG° predicts that very little dissolves.
Common mistakeMixing J and kJ is the most common error. In class answers, check that ΔG° is converted to J mol⁻¹ before dividing by RT; e.g. ΔG° = −801 kJ mol⁻¹ gives an enormous K (≈ 10¹⁴⁰), not 1.38. Also remember that K from ΔG° is at the stated temperature only.

Class question set (298 K; find ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS°, then K). An earlier answer key forgot to convert kJ to J, so its K values (1.38, 1.15, 1.04) are wrong; the corrected values are below.

1. CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(g): ΔH° = −802.5 kJ, ΔS° = −4 J K⁻¹. Calculate ΔG° in kJ mol⁻¹.

ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS° = −802.5 − 298 × (−0.004) = −801.3 kJ mol⁻¹ (ΔS converted to kJ K⁻¹).
ln K = 801 300 ÷ (8.31 × 298) = 323.6, so K ≈ e323.6 ≈ 10¹⁴⁰: the reaction goes completely to products.

2. P₄O₁₀(s) + 6H₂O(l) → 4H₃PO₄(s): ΔH° = −416 kJ, ΔS° = −209 J K⁻¹. Calculate ln K at 298 K.

ΔG° = −416 − 298 × (−0.209) = −353.7 kJ mol⁻¹ = −353 700 J mol⁻¹.
ln K = 353 700 ÷ (8.31 × 298) = 142.8, so K ≈ 10⁶² (not 1.15).

3. HCl(g) + NH₃(g) → NH₄Cl(s): ΔH° = −176 kJ, ΔS° = −284 J K⁻¹. Calculate ln K at 298 K.

ΔG° = −176 − 298 × (−0.284) = −176 + 84.6 = −91.4 kJ mol⁻¹ (the earlier answer key wrote ÷ for × but got the right ΔG°).
ln K = 91 400 ÷ (8.31 × 298) = 36.9, so K = e36.9 ≈ 1 × 10¹⁶ (not 1.04).
Assess this class example: "Ni(s) + Cl₂(g) → NiCl₂(s), ΔH = −305.3 kJ mol⁻¹, ΔS = −155.21 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. At 10 K, ΔG = −303.75 kJ mol⁻¹; −ΔG/RT = 303.75 ÷ (8.314 × 10) = 3.65; K = e3.65 = 38.5, so the reaction is favoured but not heavily." Find the error, then reveal.ΔG was left in kJ while R is in J. The correct value is −ΔG/RT = 303 750 ÷ (8.314 × 10) ≈ 3650, so K ≈ e3650: overwhelmingly favoured, not "38.5". At a realistic 298 K, ΔG° = −305.3 − 298 × (−0.15521) = −259.0 kJ mol⁻¹ and ln K = 259 000 ÷ (8.31 × 298) = 104.6, so K ≈ 10⁴⁵. Any ΔG° of hundreds of kJ means K is astronomically large or small.

IB question: for H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g) at 761 K, [H₂] = 8.72 × 10⁻⁴, [I₂] = 2.72 × 10⁻³ and [HI] = 1.04 × 10⁻² mol dm⁻³. Calculate ΔG° in kJ mol⁻¹.

K = [HI]² ÷ ([H₂][I₂]) = (1.04 × 10⁻²)² ÷ (8.72 × 10⁻⁴ × 2.72 × 10⁻³) = 45.6.
ΔG° = −RT ln K = −0.00831 kJ K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ × 761 K × ln 45.6 = −6.32 × 3.82 = −24.2 kJ mol⁻¹.

Link to Le Châtelier: at equilibrium the mixture has the minimum possible Gibbs energy. Any mixture with Q ≠ K has a higher G, and the reaction moves spontaneously towards equilibrium; that is why Q < K gives net forward reaction.

When ΔG° is negative, K is greater than 1.
